info.title: EAMS API
info.description:
Events Attendance Monitoring System — attendance capture and administration.

**This document supersedes `docs/api/attendance-contract-handoff.md` as the contract.**
It is generated from the source, so the outcome tokens, status codes and payload shapes
below are what the running build actually does.

- **Base path** `/api/v1`. JSON in and out, camelCase field names.
- **All timestamps are UTC**, ISO 8601, with an explicit `Z`. A bare or offset-bearing
  local time misjudges the Present/Late boundary by the server's offset.
- **Errors are RFC 7807** `application/problem+json`. Every body carries a `traceId` to
  quote back and, on the attendance surface, a stable `code` to branch on — never the
  human-readable `title` or `detail`, which are reworded freely.
- **Capture endpoints require a device key** (`DeviceKey` below).
- **The `/auth` endpoints sign a person in** and issue a `Bearer` access token (`Bearer`
  below). Three of them require one.
- **Everything else is still open.** A login existing is not the same as authorization
  being enforced: the roster, the events, the import pipeline and the dashboard accept
  an uncredentialed request today. Enforcing permissions across that surface is a later
  phase (ADR-001 D-6), so **an endpoint with no `Auth` marked is not a public endpoint,
  it is an unprotected one** — this API must stay on a local or trusted network.

See the `TapOutcomeCode`, `ManualOutcomeCode` and `LiveOutcomeCode` schemas for the frozen
token tables.

get.summary: `GET /academic/terms` — every term, current first and then newest first.
get.description:
The order is deliberate and does not depend on `startsOn`: the roster source has no term
date columns at all, so those two fields are frequently null and sorting on them would produce
an arbitrary list on real data. Term codes are operator-authored and sort chronologically by
construction, which is what this falls back to.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number, default 1. Out-of-range values are clamped, not refused.

parameters.name: pageSize
parameters.description: Rows per page. Default 50, maximum 200; a larger value is clamped and the response says so.

200.description: One page of terms, possibly empty.

post.description: The one academic row a human authors rather than imports. It has no source in the roster file and every import requires one to exist first, so without this route a fresh installation's only path to a term was hand-written SQL. The other four entity families behind this controller stay read-only — see the controller remarks. The new term is never current. Moving that flag is `PATCH /academic/terms/{id}/current`, which is a two-row operation under a filtered unique index rather than a field write; the create body carries no `isCurrent` at all. `code` is unique per school and a duplicate is a 409, never a 500. The body carries `code: "TermCodeExists"`. The check is made before the insert and the unique index is caught as well, because those are two statements and a second operator creating the same code in the same second is decided by the index.

requestBody.description: The term's code, school year, semester and optional calendar dates.

201.description: The created term. `Location` names the term list — see below.

400.description: A field is blank, over-length, whitespace-padded, or the dates run backwards.

409.description:
A term with this code already exists in this school, or no school could be resolved to file it
under.

get.summary: `GET /academic/terms/current` — the term flagged current, or 404 when none is.
get.description: 404 rather than a 200 carrying null, because the two are different facts and a client has to act on them differently. "No term is flagged current" is a configuration state an administrator fixes — it happens between semesters, before anyone has moved the flag — whereas an empty 200 body reads as "here is the current term, it just has no fields". A caller defaulting a term picker needs to tell those apart to know whether to prompt. At most one term can be current, and the database is what guarantees it — a filtered unique index, not a convention. Two "current" terms would make every term-defaulting query pick one at random, which surfaces months later as a report quietly about the wrong semester.

404.description: No term in this school is flagged current.

put.description: A full replacement of the term's own fields: `code`, `schoolYear`, `semester` and the two optional dates. It does not move the current-term flag — that is `PATCH /academic/terms/{id}/current`, and a display edit silently redefining which semester the institution is in is exactly the side effect the split exists to prevent. `code` is editable, and renaming onto another term's code is a 409. Fixing a typo in a code is the most likely edit anyone makes here. What a rename does not rewrite: derived `StudentGroup` display names embed the code at projection time (`"BSFS 2-A (2025-2026-1)"`) and keep the old text until the next import re-runs the projection — stale wording, not a wrong audience, since groups resolve on ids.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The term.

400.description: A field is blank, over-length, whitespace-padded, or the dates run backwards.

409.description: Another term in this school already holds that code.

patch.summary: `PATCH /academic/terms/{id}/current` — make this the current term, or retire it (D-53).
patch.description: Its own route rather than an `isCurrent` field on the PUT, for the same reason `PATCH /events/{id}/status` is its own route. `IsCurrent` is not a property of the row, it is a claim about the school: a filtered unique index (`UNIQUE(SchoolId) WHERE IsCurrent = 1`) caps it at one term per school, so setting it clears whichever term holds it — a two-row transaction, not a field write. A PUT carrying the flag would be one resource's payload silently rewriting a different resource, and it would fail or no-op depending on which term happened to be current at the time. `isCurrent` is required, and omitting it is a 400 rather than a default. A missing JSON member would bind to `false` and quietly retire the school's term. Send `{"isCurrent": true}` to make this term current, or `{"isCurrent": false}` to retire it — which is the only retirement there is, since D-53 offers no deletion. Retiring leaves the school with no current term, an ordinary state the reads already answer for. Idempotent: setting a term that is already current, or clearing one that is not, changes nothing and answers 200.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The term.

200.description: The term, with its new flag. Exactly one term per school can carry it.

get.summary: `GET /academic/colleges` — every college, by name.
get.description:
Unfiltered, and paged like every other admin list — a college list really is a handful of rows
per institution, but "this table is small today" is a property of the data rather than of the
endpoint, and the two lists on this controller that were argued unbounded on exactly that
reasoning (offerings, groups) are the two that grew per term. `code` is nullable: the
roster source has no college code column, so the natural key is the normalized name and the
code exists only to be filled in later.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number, default 1. Out-of-range values are clamped, not refused.

parameters.name: pageSize
parameters.description: Rows per page. Default 50, maximum 200; a larger value is clamped and the response says so.

200.description: One page of colleges, possibly empty.

get.summary: `GET /academic/programs` — degree programmes, optionally narrowed to one college.

parameters.name: collegeId
parameters.description:
Omit to list them all. An id matching no college returns an empty list rather than everything —
a filter that silently stops filtering is how an "invite this college" flow ends up inviting
the institution.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number, default 1. Out-of-range values are clamped, not refused.

parameters.name: pageSize
parameters.description: Rows per page. Default 50, maximum 200; a larger value is clamped and the response says so.

200.description: One page of matching programmes, possibly empty.

get.summary: `GET /academic/courses` — courses, optionally narrowed by college and search term.

parameters.name: collegeId
parameters.description:
Omit to list them all. A course's college is itself nullable, so an unattributed course matches
no `collegeId` — which is correct: it is not known to be in one, rather than known not to
be.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Matched against both the code and the title. A user typing "criminology" is naming the title while one typing "SSCI" is naming the code, and asking which they meant is worse than searching both. Substring, case-insensitive by the database's collation.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number, default 1. Out-of-range values are clamped, not refused.

parameters.name: pageSize
parameters.description: Rows per page. Default 50, maximum 200; a larger value is clamped and the response says so.

200.description: One page of matching courses, possibly empty.

get.summary: `GET /academic/course-offerings` — the section grain, and the row an audience picker is really looking for. A course taught to two sections is two entries.
get.description: This is the endpoint that answers "who is in BSCRIM 2-A", and `students.section` is not. That column is the ADR-001 D-2 derived display cache: it is single-valued, and twelve of the fifty-two students in the real roster sit in more than one section, so it is wrong for roughly a quarter of them. An offering is the grain an invitation is actually issued at. `sectionKey` is published alongside `sectionName` because a cohort has no row of its own — it is a key shared by every offering that cohort takes within a term, which is why the group projection keys section groups on it. `sectionName` is null where the source was blank (39 sample rows are); the key is a sentinel rather than null in that case, because a nullable key component would have capped the table at one blank section under SQL Server's unique index.

parameters.name: termId
parameters.description: Omit to get the current term, not every term. Section names repeat each semester against a different cohort, so an unscoped list stacked several distinct audiences under identical names and grew with every import the institution had ever run — this endpoint returned every offering of every term, which is the defect the default closes. When no term is flagged current, the response is an empty page. Zero current terms is a real state — the flag is capped at one per school, not pinned at one, and between semesters nobody has moved it yet. Widening back to every term in that case would restore the unbounded read on the one day nobody is watching for it. Ask `GET /academic/terms/current` to tell "no offerings this term" from "no term is current"; it 404s on the second.

parameters.name: courseId
parameters.description: Omit to list offerings of every course in the scoped term.

parameters.name: section
parameters.description: The section's display name. Normalized before it is compared — `BSFS 2-A`, `bsfs2a` and `BSFS-2A` are one section — so the filter does not depend on how the caller happened to type it.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: 1-based page number, default 1. Out-of-range values are clamped, not refused.

parameters.name: pageSize
parameters.description: Rows per page. Default 50, maximum 200; a larger value is clamped and the response says so.

200.description:
One page of matching offerings, possibly empty — including when no term is flagged current and
none was named.

get.summary: `GET /attendance` — recorded attendance rows, every filter optional.
get.description: A back-office read rather than something to poll: offset-paged, newest check-in first. The live dashboard's read is `GET /attendance/live/{eventId}`, which is cursored. The two are not variations on one endpoint and must not be made into one. This answers "give me rows 40 to 60 of what matched"; the live one answers "what changed after this cursor", and its `since`/`cursor`/`hasMore` shape is frozen published contract (D-29/D-30/D-42) that a mobile client polls today. Offset paging over a live feed also loses rows outright — an insert below the offset shifts everything up by one and the next page skips it — which is exactly why that endpoint was built on a `rowversion` cursor instead.

parameters.name: eventId
parameters.description: Restrict to one event.

parameters.name: studentId
parameters.description: Restrict to one student.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: One of `Present`, `Late`, `Absent`, `Excused`.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description:
1-based page number, default 1. Out-of-range values are clamped, never refused; the response
echoes the page actually served.

parameters.name: pageSize
parameters.description:
Rows per page. Default 50, maximum 200 — a larger value is clamped to the maximum and the
response says so in its own `pageSize`.

200.description: One page of matching rows, possibly empty. Never a 404 for an empty filter.

post.description: One tap, decided by the same function every row of `POST /attendance/tap/batch` goes through. Resolve the card UID → check the event and its window → absorb a replay by `deviceTapId` → write or update the row → decide Present versus Late from `tappedAt` and the event's `graceMinutes`. Branch on `code`, never on `message`. The token set and the status each one arrives with are frozen contract — see the `TapOutcomeCode` schema. A success is a `TapResult`; a rejection is an RFC 7807 body carrying the same `code` and `serverTime`, so one accessor reads both. Always send a `deviceTapId`, and never regenerate it on retry. It is optional here and required on the batch endpoint, but it is what makes a lost response recoverable: a replay comes back `DuplicateIgnored` instead of writing a second row. Send an explicit `tappedAt` too. With `null` the instant being validated is re-derived from our clock on every attempt, so a tap that landed at 10:00 and is retried at 12:30 — after the event's window closed — comes back `400 TappedAtOutsideEventWindow` rather than the `DuplicateIgnored` you would expect. The stored row is correct either way; only reconciliation by code is wrong for it.

requestBody.description: The tap. See `TapRequest` for the per-field rules.

401.description: No device key, or one that is malformed or unknown.

403.description: The key was revoked, or the device was retired.

200.description:
`Recorded`, `DuplicateIgnored`, `CheckedOut` or `AlreadyRecorded`. All four
             mean the client can drop the tap from its queue.

400.description:
`EventNotOpen`, `DeviceMismatch`, `TappedAtOutOfRange` or
             `TappedAtOutsideEventWindow`. Stop retrying — the same request will be refused forever.

404.description:
`EventNotFound`, `CardNotFound` or `DeviceNotRegistered`. The last also covers a
             device belonging to another school — deliberately indistinguishable.

post.description: A well-formed batch is always 200, never 207. The transport status describes the batch; each row's own `status` describes that tap. 207 Multi-Status is handled inconsistently by proxies and client libraries, and — the part that bites — a client seeing any non-2xx is liable to retry the entire batch, which is safe but pure waste when almost all of it landed. The fourth and last endpoint a device key gates (D-28). `[HasPermissionNotEnforced]` stays alongside `[Authorize]` for the reason the tap endpoint records: the inert attribute is the list Phase 6's rename walks, and the enforced-first endpoints are the ones a reader is least likely to check. The `Policy` is named rather than left to the default — a bare `[Authorize]` falls back to `RequireAuthenticatedUser()`, which a revoked key and a deactivated device both satisfy by design, so it would admit exactly the credentials the 403 exists to refuse. `AuthorizationSeamTests` fails the build on either mistake. Two size guards, and neither replaces the other. `[RequestSizeLimit]` refuses an oversized body before it is buffered; EAMS.Domain.TapBatchLimits.MaxRows is checked in the service after deserialization, when the row count is knowable. A body of 200 enormous rows passes the first and fails nothing; a body of one row and four megabytes of whitespace passes the second. It shares `/tap`'s rate-limit policy, so one flush of 200 taps spends one permit where 200 single taps would spend 200. That is intended, and it is recorded because nothing else would say so. The limiter's stated purpose is friction and detection against a runaway client, not a contractual quota on taps — and a device that batches is being well behaved, so charging it per row would penalise the shape §8.2 asks for and make the published {PermitsPerWindow}-per-minute figure mean two different things depending on which endpoint was used. What it does mean, stated plainly: the effective per-device write ceiling on this endpoint is `PermitsPerWindow × MaxRows` — 120,000 taps a minute — so the limiter is not what bounds batch write volume. The row cap and the body cap are. If a per-row budget is ever wanted, it needs a token-bucket policy that charges by row count, which the fixed-window limiter cannot express.

401.description: No device key, or one that is malformed or unknown.

403.description: The key was revoked, or the device was retired.

429.description: Capture rate limit. One flush spends one permit, whatever its row count.

200.description: Every well-formed batch, including an empty one. `results` is dense — one entry per submitted tap, in the order you sent them, so `results[i].index == i` and `accepted + rejected == results.length`. Each row's own `status` is the status that tap would have received as a single `POST /attendance/tap`. On a `5xx`, retry the whole batch — that is always safe. Safe because every row is idempotent, not because the batch is atomic: rows commit individually, so a server error partway through leaves the earlier rows written and the retry absorbs them as `DuplicateIgnored`.

400.description:
Transport or size only: a malformed body, or `BatchTooLarge`. The refusal echoes the limit
as `maxBatchRows` in the problem body, so chunk from the response rather than hard-coding
the number. Nothing about the content of an individual row can produce a batch-level 4xx.

get.summary:
`GET /attendance/live/{eventId}` — the D-29 cursor-delta poll that stands in for §5/§6.4's
             SignalR hub. Omit `since` for a snapshot; send back the previous response's `cursor`
             for the changes since it.
get.description: The permission is `attendance.read` and there is deliberately no `[Authorize]`. This is a dashboard read, not a capture, and the only authentication scheme that exists today is the device key — which §11 scopes to `attendance.capture` and nothing else. Gating this endpoint with it would force the admin SPA to hold a capture-scoped credential in a browser in order to watch attendance, which inverts the split §6.4 draws between capturing and reading and would hand a page that can only display data a key that can write it. It stays open under ADR-001 D-6 with the rest of the admin surface, declares the permission Phase 6 will enforce, and is listed alongside `GET /attendance` — the endpoint it is a live view of — rather than alongside the tap. `Cache-Control: no-store`. A cached delta is worse than a slow one: an intermediary replaying a 200 for a cursor the client has already advanced past would make the dashboard silently stop updating, and the client has no way to tell that from an event where nothing is happening. `no-store` rather than `no-cache` because there is nothing here worth revalidating — every response is keyed to a cursor that will never be asked for again.

parameters.name: eventId
parameters.description: The event to watch.

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Omit for a snapshot; otherwise the `cursor` from your previous response, verbatim. Opaque — store it, send it back, never parse it. A blank value is treated as absent.

200.description: Exactly one of `entries` (you sent no cursor — replace your state) or `changes` (you sent one — merge). The other key is omitted entirely rather than sent as null. Do not ignore `hasMore`. A response carries at most 500 rows; when it is true the page was truncated and you should poll again immediately rather than waiting `pollAfterSeconds`. Otherwise a 5,000-attendee event takes ten polls to fill a dashboard and looks broken rather than paging. `counters` is `GET /events/{id}/summary`'s own object — the same numbers from the same query, bounded by the same cursor ceiling as the rows beside them.

400.description:
`InvalidCursor`. Re-poll with no `since`. Refused rather than silently downgraded to a
             snapshot, which would look like "nothing changed" forever while your cursor stayed broken.

429.description:
240 polls per minute per client address — about one every 250 ms, far above the 5-second
default. Partitioned separately from device-key capture limits, so a dashboard tab can never
spend a kiosk's tap budget.

post.description: Not a device path. It carries `attendance.write` rather than the tap's `attendance.capture`: a kiosk's device key is scoped to capture only, and an override is the audited organizer action §6.4 describes. Collapsing the two permissions would let a reader rewrite a status. It keeps working on a `Closed` event, deliberately (ADR-003 D-17). Closing is terminal, and this is the only route back from a mistake — adding the tap path's status guard here reads as a safety improvement in review and turns that terminal status into a dead end. Its `code` values are their own frozen table — see the `ManualOutcomeCode` schema — and they travel through the identical `code` field a tap uses, on success bodies and RFC 7807 problem bodies alike.

parameters.name: eventId
parameters.description: The event to record against.

parameters.name: studentId
parameters.description: The student.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description:
One of §4.9's values — `Present`, `Late`, `Absent`, `Excused`. Anything else
is `400 InvalidStatus` rather than a stored value no summary can count.

parameters.name: notes
parameters.description:
Free text, at most EAMS.Domain.AttendanceNotes.MaxLength characters. Over-length is
`400 InvalidNotes` — it used to reach SQL Server and come back as a truncation 500.

400.description: `InvalidStatus` or `InvalidNotes`, as an RFC 7807 body carrying `code` and `serverTime`. Not a `TapResult` with `success: false` — that shape left the 4xx responses in Phase 4c.

post.summary:
`POST /auth/login` — exchange an e-mail address and password for an access token and a
            session.
post.description: The response sets two cookies. `eams_rt` is the refresh token: `httpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Strict`, scoped to this `/auth` path, and unreadable by any script. `eams_csrf` is readable, and the SPA must echo its value in an `X-CSRF-Token` header on `refresh` and `logout` — those two routes are the only ones in the API a browser attaches an ambient credential to. Every failure is one 401 with `code: InvalidCredentials`. Do not branch on anything finer; there is nothing finer, deliberately.

200.description: Signed in. Body carries the access token and the effective permission set.

400.description: The body is not a login request.

401.description: Unknown address, wrong password, or a deactivated account — indistinguishably.

429.description: Too many attempts, from this address or against this account. Honour `Retry-After`.

post.summary: `POST /auth/refresh` — rotate the session cookie and mint a new access token.
post.description: The request body is empty and the request is not anonymous. The refresh token is read from the `eams_rt` cookie; sending it in a body is no longer supported (drift from §6.1, see EAMS.Api.Authentication.AuthCookies). The `X-CSRF-Token` header is required and must equal the `eams_csrf` cookie. Rotation is single-use and replay burns the family. Presenting a token that has already been rotated revokes every live token in its family — the legitimate client pays one sign-in, a thief's chain dies. Do not retry a refresh with the same cookie value after a failure; take the 401 and sign in. The permission set is re-read on every refresh, so a grant changed by an administrator takes effect within one access-token lifetime rather than at the user's next sign-in.

200.description: Rotated. New cookies are set and a new access token is returned.

401.description: No session cookie, or one that is expired, unknown, or already used.

403.description: The `X-CSRF-Token` header is missing or does not match the cookie.

429.description: Too many requests from this address. Honour `Retry-After`.

post.description: This session only. Signing out on a laptop does not sign the user out on their phone. The operation that ends every session is `POST /auth/change-password`, which is what a user reaches for when they believe a credential has leaked. Requires a Bearer token and the `X-CSRF-Token` header. It is idempotent: a logout that presents no session cookie revokes nothing and still answers 204 with the cookies cleared, because the postcondition — this browser is signed out — holds either way.

204.description: Signed out. Both cookies are cleared.

401.description: No Bearer token, or one that is expired or malformed.

403.description: The `X-CSRF-Token` header is missing or does not match the cookie.

get.summary: `GET /auth/me` — who this access token speaks for, and what it may do.
get.description: The permissions come from the token, not from a fresh database read, and that is the whole point of the endpoint. The server will enforce what this token carries for as long as it lives, so a UI that gates its navigation on anything else will eventually show a button the server refuses or hide one it would have allowed. A grant changed by an administrator appears here after the next `POST /auth/refresh` — at most one access-token lifetime away. The display fields are read from the database, because a name and an address are not access decisions and do not belong in a token that travels in a header on every request.

401.description: No Bearer token, or one that is expired or malformed.

404.description: The token is valid and the account behind it no longer is.

post.summary: `POST /auth/change-password` — change the caller's own password and end every session.
post.description: Requires the current password even though the caller holds a valid token. A token is what someone who walked past an unlocked laptop has; the current password is what only the account holder has, and this is the operation that would lock the real owner out. Every refresh token for this user is revoked, including the caller's own. The reason to change a password is usually that it may have leaked, and a rotation that leaves other sessions live changes nothing for whoever holds one. The caller's access token keeps working until it expires — up to fifteen minutes — and then cannot be renewed. Sign in again.

204.description: Changed. Every session, including this one, has been revoked.

401.description: No Bearer token, or the current password did not verify.

422.description: The new password failed the rules a created account is held to.

429.description: Too many requests from this address. Honour `Retry-After`.

get.summary: `GET /devices` — every registered device in this school.
get.description: No key material, ever. The plaintext exists only in the 201 that issued it; this returns the public key id and the lifecycle timestamps an operator needs to decide whether a credential is still in use.

post.summary: §6.6 `POST /devices` — register, and issue the first key.
post.description: The 201 body is the only time this key is ever readable. The server stores `SHA-256(secret)` and nothing else, so there is no "show it again" endpoint to write and none to forget to protect. An operator who loses it rotates.

get.summary: `GET /devices/{id}` — one registered device.
get.description: No key material, ever — same rule as the list. The plaintext key exists only in the 201 that issued it; what comes back here is the public key id and the lifecycle timestamps.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The device.

404.description: No such device in this school.

put.summary:
§6.6 `PUT /devices/{id}` — the device's own fields. Never touches the key; see
`Device.ApiKeyRevokedAt` for why retiring a device and burning its credential are two
different statements.

post.summary:
§6.6 `POST /devices/{id}/regenerate-key` — hard cut, no overlap window. The previous key
stops working the moment this returns.
`POST /devices/{id}/revoke-key` — burn the credential without issuing a replacement.
post.description: Not defined by §6.6, and added deliberately. §6.6 offers only regeneration, which conflates "this key is compromised" with "give me a working one" — but the published mobile contract already distinguishes the two on the wire (`401` bad key versus `403` revoked key), and without this route that 403 is unreachable and `Devices.ApiKeyRevokedAt` is a column nothing can write. Recorded as drift. Idempotent: revoking twice, or revoking a device that never held a key, is a 200. The postcondition — this device cannot authenticate — holds either way, so a retry after a timeout is safe on the one operation an operator runs when something has gone wrong.

post.summary:
§6.6 `POST /devices/{id}/heartbeat` — liveness, and one of the four endpoints a device key
authenticates.
post.description: The route id must be the authenticated device's own — the same D-26 rule the tap path applies, and it took a second look to see that it belongs here too. The first version of this action skipped the check, on the reasoning that one kiosk stamping a sibling's `LastSeenAt` within its own school is a wrong liveness reading rather than a data-integrity problem. That undercounts what this writes: M:EAMS.Application.Abstractions.IDeviceService.HeartbeatAsync(System.Guid,System.Threading.CancellationToken) also sets `ApiKeyLastUsedAt`, and that column is the signal an operator reads when deciding whether a credential is still in use and therefore whether it is safe to revoke. A retired-but-not-revoked kiosk that a neighbour keeps making look active is a key that never gets burned. The check is shorter than the paragraph that argued against it. 404, not 403. A device asking about a device that is not itself learns only that the URL names nothing it can see — the same non-disclosure rule D-27 applies when it reuses `DeviceNotRegistered` rather than inventing a cross-tenant 403.

get.summary:
`GET /events/{id}/manifest` — the offline capture cache: who is expected at this event and
             which card resolves to whom.
get.description: This is the invitation, not the roster. It carries nothing about who has already tapped — that is `GET /attendance/live/{eventId}` — because a manifest carrying attendance state would read as authoritative on the device, and the one thing this object must never be is authoritative. Offline validation against it is display-only and never gating. A tap whose card UID is absent from the manifest must still be queued and flushed. The server rules on it and it lands as a walk-in (`isExpected: false`). A client that refuses to capture an unknown card turns "my cache is stale" into "that attendance never happened", and afterwards the two are indistinguishable. Send the previous `version` back as `If-None-Match` on every pull. Unchanged is a `304` with no body — keep what you have. The comparison is weak (`W/`) and lenient about quoting, so sending the header back verbatim always works. Never parse the version and never order it; compare it for equality only. Check `serverTime` against the device clock before enabling scan mode: more than five minutes apart, do not scan. Every tap captured past that threshold arrives as `TappedAtOutOfRange` — poison, dropped by your own queue, attendance gone. A `304` carries no `serverTime`; take the offset from the HTTP `Date` header instead, because the manifest not changing says nothing about the clock. Two obligations that hold across every response, including the failures. Never clear the cached manifest on a failure — a client that wipes on error degrades from slightly-stale names to no names, and does it exactly when the network is worst; the only sanctioned discard is after the queue drains on a terminal event. And no refusal here ever stops tap capture: capture and queueing continue whatever this endpoint returns. Only the flush pauses, and only on `401` or `403`. Read the HTTP status first and `code` second; never branch on `title` or `detail`. Only `EventFrozen` and `ManifestTooLarge` are new tokens — the rest are the ones the capture path already uses, with the same meanings. Event-scoped, not occurrence-scoped. §4.8 `EventGroups` carries no `OccurrenceId`, so one manifest serves every occurrence of a recurring event and `startAt`/`endAt` are the template's. Recurrence is unbuilt; an `occurrenceId` parameter is additive when it lands.

It mirrors `TapBatchRequest.clientClockAt` exactly, and its value is that it is the same quantity as flush-time skew measured hours earlier: a device that pulls at 08:00 and flushes at 15:00 gives us no drift signal for seven hours, during which every tap it captured is already unrecoverable.

The comparison is weak (`W/`) and lenient about spelling: `W/"m1.abc"`, `"m1.abc"`,

comparison defined on it.

changes. It is **not** ordered and carries no time: compare it for equality only.

credential, not of the URL.

One that resolves to nobody is a `CardNotFound` rejection - an HTTP response and nothing more - so before this report existed, "nobody scanned" and "somebody scanned a card we could not place" were the same absence of evidence. The second is the one worth investigating, and it was the one being discarded. `events.read` rather than `attendance.read`: it is read from the event page, beside the roster it completes, and a permission split that puts half of one screen behind a second grant is a permission split nobody configures correctly.

ADR-001 D-6 left every read open until §11 could be applied to all of them at once; this one arrives after the login exists, is consumed by nothing yet, and is unreachable by any device key - the mobile surface is five DeviceKey routes and this is not among them. So it can be gated without breaking a caller, which makes it the cheapest possible place to prove the machinery before the rest of §11 follows. Bearer only. A device key is scoped to `attendance.capture` and has no business reading a report; binding the policy to a scheme rather than to a claim alone is what stops a capture credential satisfying an operator's permission. post.summary: `POST /events/audience/resolve` — how many students a filter matches, who they are, and a preview (D-50/D-51). A read that writes nothing, despite the verb.
post.description: Read-only and idempotent. It resolves an audience; it does not attach one, does not touch an event, and can be called on every keystroke of a filter builder. `POST` rather than `GET` because the filter set is a structured body — a list of rows, each with a list of values — which outgrows a query string as fields are added, and encoding it into one would make the encoding part of the contract. Not under `/events/{id}`, because it is not about an event. It is the query the create-event screen runs before there is an event to attach anything to, and pinning it to an id would force the UI to create a draft in order to count. Five fields, and the list is closed on purpose. `College`, `Program`, `YearLevel`, `Section`, `Course` — each resolving through `StudentTermRecords` or `Enrollments`. The student record's own `course`/`yearLevel`/`section` columns are unreachable from here by construction: they are the ADR-001 D-2 display cache, they are single-valued, and 12 of the 52 students in the real roster sit in more than one section — so a section filter reading them returns a plausible, non-empty, incomplete answer. See EAMS.Domain.AudienceField. Values within a row union; rows intersect (D-51). `Year is any of 2, 3` plus `Program is BSIT` is `(year 2 or 3) and BSIT`. A row with no values is ignored rather than treated as "match nobody" — it is a half-finished edit. An unregistered field is `400 UnknownAudienceField` and a value the field cannot hold is `400 InvalidAudienceFilterValue`; neither is ever silently dropped, because a filter that vanishes reports a count nobody asked for. At most twenty rows per request — EAMS.Domain.AudienceResolutionLimits.MaxFilterRows. More is `400 TooManyFilterRows`, refused before the term is resolved and before anything is read. There are only five filterable fields, so twenty is four times what naming each of them once costs; past that each extra row is another condition the database has to plan, and enough of them compose a query the server cannot plan at all. The excess rows are refused rather than dropped for the same reason as everything above: rows narrow each other, so ignoring one widens the audience. `count` describes exactly what the filter matches and is bounded by nothing. `studentIds` is capped, and when the cap bites `studentIdsTruncated` says so — see EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto for why this response publishes a number larger than the list under it rather than a list that quietly describes less than the number.

On a live event (`Draft`/`Open`) it lists the individually-attached students. On a terminal event (`Closed` or `Cancelled` — `isFrozen: true`) it is empty by contract: the freeze wrote the entire resolved audience down as individual rows, so returning them here would duplicate the roster in an unbounded response. Empty there does not mean nobody was attached. The per-student frozen set is `GET /events/{id}/roster`; `expected` and `groups` carry the size and the cohort. `groups` is returned whatever the status. On a terminal event those rows are the historical record of which cohort was invited — nothing resolves them any more, and keeping them is the reason the freeze does not delete them.

Offset paging over a live feed also drops rows: an insert below the cursor shifts every subsequent row up by one and the next page skips it. The two mechanisms coexisting is correct, not an inconsistency to tidy.

cursor.description: Opaque. Store it, send it back as `?since=`, do not parse it. See `EAMS.Domain.AttendanceCursor` for what is inside and why. It advances even when nothing changed, because it is a ceiling on what has been read rather than the high-water mark of what was returned. Echoing the caller's own cursor back on an empty delta would leave every poll re-scanning the same range forever after a quiet event.

pollAfterSeconds.description: How long the client should wait before polling again. In the body on purpose: it lets the server back every dashboard off under load without anyone shipping a client release, which is the one operational lever a polling design has and a hub does not.

hasMore.description: True when this response was truncated at EAMS.Application.Abstractions.AttendanceLiveOptions.MaxPageRows and more rows are already available below EAMS.Application.Dtos.AttendanceLiveDto.Cursor. Poll again immediately rather than waiting EAMS.Application.Dtos.AttendanceLiveDto.PollAfterSeconds. Without this the page cap would be its own defect: a five-thousand-row first snapshot at five hundred rows a page and five seconds between pages takes the better part of a minute to fill a dashboard that used to fill in one request. The flag costs one boolean and turns the cap into paging.

AttendanceLiveDto.description: The body of `GET /attendance/live/{eventId}` — cursor-delta polling in place of the §5/§6.4 SignalR hub (Phase 4d, D-29). Why polling, recorded here because the endpoint is the argument. A hub client has to fetch a snapshot on every reconnect to close the gap it missed, so an endpoint of exactly this shape is required under both designs — the hub would have been the second mechanism, not the first. Polling also needs no backplane and no sticky sessions, survives a campus firewall, and keeps a device key out of a WebSocket query string where it lands in access logs. One type serves both calls, and exactly one of the two collections is present.EAMS.Application.Dtos.AttendanceLiveDto.Entries when the caller sent no cursor, EAMS.Application.Dtos.AttendanceLiveDto.Changes when it sent one; the absent one is omitted from the JSON entirely rather than serialized as `null`, so the two published shapes are byte-for-byte what the document describes. The distinction is not cosmetic — a client that received `{entries: [...], changes: null}` would have to guess which mode it is in, and the whole point of the split is that a snapshot replaces state while a delta merges into it.

field.description: One of five values — `College`, `Program`, `YearLevel`, `Section`, `Course` — matched case-insensitively. See EAMS.Domain.AudienceField for the whole registry and for why the list is closed rather than open over the student columns. Anything else is `400 UnknownAudienceField`, never a row that is quietly skipped. A filter that vanishes produces a count that is larger than the operator asked for, looks entirely normal, and is invisible until the wrong people are standing in a hall.

values.description: The values selected on this field — ids for `College`, `Program` and `Course`, the bare year digit for `YearLevel`, the section key for `Section`. Within one row the values union; across rows they intersect (D-51).`Year is any of 2, 3` matches 2nd or 3rd years; adding `Program is BSIT` narrows that to 2nd- and 3rd-year BSIT students. Two rows naming the same field intersect like any other pair, because a row is a row — `Year in (2,3)` and `Year in (3,4)` resolves to year 3. An empty or absent list makes the row a no-op, not "match nobody". An empty-but-present row is a half-finished edit, and resolving it to zero would collapse the count to nothing while the operator is still choosing values. The field is still validated: `{"field": "Nickname", "values": []}` is a 400. A value the field cannot express is `400 InvalidAudienceFilterValue`; a well-formed value that matches nobody is simply an empty answer. The line is between the two kinds of wrong: a college id that is not a GUID is a type error the caller can only have made by mistake, whereas a perfectly good id naming a college that no longer exists is the same "filter matched nothing" every other read in this system already answers with an empty list. The blank string is refused on every field, and on `Section` so is the `(unspecified)` sentinel — both when it is sent verbatim, as `GET /academic/course-offerings` publishes it for a blank-section offering, and when a blank value normalizes onto it. That key means "the source recorded no section", it is the one audience `POST /events/{id}/attendees` refuses as `NotACohort`, and the builder must not be a way around that.

AudienceFilterDto.description: One row of the filter builder: a field, and the values selected on it.

termId.description:
The term this resolution was actually computed against — the one requested, or the current one when
none was. `null` means no term could be resolved, in which case every other field is empty; see
EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolveRequest.TermId.

count.description: How many students the filter matches. It is never bounded by anything below it. This is the number the builder shows and the number an operator acts on, so it is a `COUNT(*)` over the composed filter and not the length of EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.StudentIds. The distinction is D-42's: the live endpoint once published counters bounded by its read ceiling rather than by what it had actually returned, and the result was a headline number describing rows nobody received — internally consistent, entirely plausible, wrong. If EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.StudentIds is short, this field is why, and EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.StudentIdsTruncated says so.

studentIds.description: The matched students, ordered by student number then id — a total order, so two identical requests return the same list in the same sequence. Bounded by EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.StudentIdLimit, and the bound is announced rather than inferred. When EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.StudentIdsTruncated is `true` this is the first EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.StudentIdLimit of that ordering and EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.Count is the real size. Do not attach an audience by posting a truncated list back — an attach re-runs the filter server-side (D-52), which is the only way the invited set and the previewed count can be the same set.

studentIdsTruncated.description:
Whether EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.StudentIds is shorter than EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.Count. Published as its own flag
rather than left for a client to derive by comparing lengths: the comparison is easy to forget, and
forgetting it is silent.

studentIdLimit.description:
The ceiling EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.StudentIds was cut at, whether or not it was reached. Echoed so a caller
can size its own behaviour against the server's actual limit instead of a number compiled into it.

sample.description: The first few matched students, with names — the "[ Preview ]" list. It is a prefix of EAMS.Application.Dtos.AudienceResolutionDto.StudentIds, from the same ordering in the same query shape, so the first name in the preview is the first id in the list.

AudienceResolutionDto.description: What a filter set resolves to: how many students match, who they are, and enough of them to preview. A student in two matching sections is counted once. That is the ADR-001 D-2 tripwire and the reason this endpoint exists at all rather than a query over `Students.Section`. It holds structurally rather than by a `DISTINCT` bolted on the end: the resolution is rooted in `StudentTermRecords`, which carries exactly one row per student per term, and the section and course filters are existence tests over `Enrollments` that cannot multiply it.

termId.description: Optional, and omitting it means the term flagged `IsCurrent` — not "every term". The default follows `IAcademicReferenceService.ListCourseOfferingsAsync`, which is the endpoint this builder's section and course values come from, and it follows it for the same reason: section names repeat every semester against an entirely different cohort, so an unscoped resolution would stack several distinct audiences under identical names and grow with every import the institution has ever run. It also keeps the create-event screen honest — the §4 mock-up has a filter builder and no term picker, so a required `termId` would be a field the UI has nowhere to get. filters.description: The rows of the builder. Null or empty resolves the whole term — which is the operator's "or all", not a malformed request. Capped at EAMS.Domain.AudienceResolutionLimits.MaxFilterRows rows; more is `400 TooManyFilterRows`. Five fields are filterable, so twenty rows is four times what naming each of them once costs — the ceiling is reachable only by a caller who is composing a query rather than describing an audience. The rows past it are refused rather than dropped, because rows narrow each other and a dropped row can only widen the audience.

AudienceResolveRequest.description: The body of `POST /events/audience/resolve` — a term and a set of filter rows.

AudienceStudentDto.description:
One student in a resolution preview. Identity and a display name, and deliberately nothing else —
this is a filter preview, not a roster read, and `section` in particular is absent because the
only single-valued answer available for it is the ADR-001 D-2 cache column this whole feature is
built to avoid reading.

accessToken.description: The signed JWT. Fifteen-minute lifetime (`JwtOptions.AccessTokenLifetime`) — its lifetime is its revocation window, which is why the long-lived half lives in a table instead.

tokenType.description:
Always `Bearer`. Present so a generated client composes the header from the response rather
than from a hard-coded string it will get wrong once.

expiresAt.description:
When AccessToken stops being accepted, UTC. The SPA refreshes ahead of this
rather than waiting for a 401 — a 401 mid-navigation is a lost page, not a renewal.

AuthTokenResponse.description: The 200 body of `POST /auth/login` and `POST /auth/refresh`. There is deliberately no `refreshToken` field here, and there was one in the §6.1 sketch. permissions.description: The permissions carried by the presented token, not a fresh read of the database. The difference matters on exactly the day it looks wrong. Permissions are baked into the access token at issue, so a grant revoked one minute ago is still honoured by a token minted two minutes ago until it expires. If this field answered from the database instead, the UI would hide a button that the server would still accept, or — far worse — show one that the server would refuse, and the user would meet a 403 the interface promised them they would not. Answering from the token makes the UI's model of what it may do exactly the server's model, for exactly as long as the token lives. A change takes effect at the next refresh, which is at most fifteen minutes away.

AuthUserDto.description:
The authenticated user, as the SPA gates its navigation on. Also the whole body of

newPassword.description:
Held to the same rules `IUserProvisioningService` applies at creation, so an account cannot
be walked below the bar it was created at.

CollegeDto.description:
A college. Code is nullable because the roster source has no college code
column at all — the natural key is the normalized name, and the code exists so a real one can be
recorded later without a migration.

items.description:
This page's rows, in the endpoint's documented order. Empty is an ordinary answer — for an empty
filter and for a page past the end alike.

page.description: The 1-based page actually served, which is not necessarily the one requested: an out-of-range `?page=` is clamped and this is where a client sees that it was.

pageSize.description:

makes clamping discoverable rather than silent.

total.description:

enrolledCount.description:
Students enrolled in this offering, excluding the soft-deleted — the size of the audience
inviting this offering would produce. Counted in the database as part of the same query, never by
loading the enrollment rows.

That column is the ADR-001 D-2 derived display cache and is single-valued; twelve of the fifty-two students in the real roster sit in more than one section, so no single-valued column can describe them. A course taught to two sections is two rows here, which is the grain an invitation is issued at. apiKeyId.description: The public half of the key — the twelve characters between `eams_dk_` and the secret. Safe to show and to log: it identifies the credential without being one, which is what makes "device 3's key id is `a91f…`, and the log line that failed says `a91f…`" a possible sentence. Null when the device has never been issued a key.

hasActiveKey.description:
Whether this device could authenticate right now: it has a key, the key is not revoked, and the
device is active. A single boolean rather than three, because "why can this kiosk not tap?" is one
question and the three columns answer it together.

DeviceDto.description: Technical Plan §4.10 / §6.6, as a client sees it. There is deliberately no key-shaped field on this record. Not the secret, not the hash, not the token. The plaintext key exists in exactly two responses — the 201 from `POST /devices` and the 200 from `POST /devices/{id}/regenerate-key` — and in EAMS.Application.Dtos.DeviceKeyIssuedDto alone. Adding a `apiKey` here to "make the list more useful" would turn every `GET /devices` into a credential dump, which is precisely why `DeviceLifecycleTests.No_read_response_ever_carries_the_key` asserts on the serialized bytes rather than on the record's shape.

apiKey.description:
The complete `eams_dk_<keyId>_<secret>` token. Frozen format — see
`docs/api/attendance-contract-handoff.md`.

DeviceKeyIssuedDto.description:
The one and only carrier of a plaintext device key.
            


Returned at issue and at rotation, and never afterwards — the server keeps only
`SHA-256(secret)`, so "show me the key again" has no implementation rather than a refused
one. An operator who loses it rotates.

DeviceWriteRequest.description: The body of `POST /devices` and `PUT /devices/{id}`. `SchoolId` is deliberately absent, exactly as it is on `EventWriteRequest`: the tenant comes from EAMS.Application.Abstractions.ISchoolContext, never from the request. A caller-supplied tenant on a write is the hole Phase 4b closed on the tap path (D-27); this surface does not open a second one. No key field either. A key is minted by the server or it is not minted — see `DeviceKey.Issue` for why an operator-chosen key would invalidate the hashing decision.

status.description: The event's §4.5 status, so a caller need not fetch the event to know it.

isFrozen.description:
True once this event's audience has been snapshotted — both terminal statuses (ADR-003 D-16). The
same flag, computed the same way, as EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventRosterDto.IsFrozen: the two cannot disagree
about one event.

expected.description: The invited population — the same number `GET /events/{id}/summary` and `GET /events/{id}/roster` report for this event, from the same query. It is deliberately not derivable from the lists below: on a live event the group members are not enumerated here, and on a terminal event EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.Students is empty by contract. A caller wanting the denominator reads this field; a caller wanting the people reads the roster.

groups.description: Every attached §4.7 group, whatever the event's status. On a terminal event these are the historical record of which cohort was invited (ADR-003 D-13) — no query resolves them any more, and they are returned precisely because that record is the thing the freeze keeps.

students.description: Its meaning depends on EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.IsFrozen, which is why that flag is published beside it. While the event is live (`Draft`/`Open`) these are the individually-attached students — the handful an organizer named by hand on top of the sections, and the exact set the `DELETE .../attendees/students/{studentId}` sub-resource addresses. Once EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.IsFrozen, this list is empty by contract, and the emptiness does not mean "no students were attached" — it means "ask elsewhere". The freeze writes the whole resolved audience down as individual rows (ADR-003 D-13), so the same query that returns three students on a live event returns the entire population, unbounded, on a terminal one. That is `GET /events/{id}/roster`'s job, and duplicating it here would add a second unbounded response where ADR-003 already carries one as an open follow-up. The per-student frozen set is `GET /events/{id}/roster`.EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.Expected and EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.Groups carry the answer for anyone who only needs the size and the cohort. Soft-deleted students are listed on a live event rather than hidden. Their §4.8 row exists and is detachable, so hiding it would leave a row no client could see and no organizer could remove, while a re-post naming that student would report it as already attached against a panel showing nothing. They are excluded from EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.Expected while the event is live regardless (ADR-003 D-15), so the two figures legitimately differ — this list is the attachment, not the denominator.

EventAudienceDto.description: `GET /events/{id}/attendees` — what is currently attached to an event's audience, as the §4.8 `EventGroups` rows themselves rather than as the population they resolve to. EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.IsFrozen is the discriminator, and reading this object without it is a mistake. It is the same predicate EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventRosterDto.IsFrozen publishes — terminal, so both `Closed` and `Cancelled`, not `Closed` alone — and it changes what EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.Students means, as that field's own documentation sets out. This is the read half of `POST /events/{id}/attendees` and the two `DELETE` sub-resources: every id it returns is one those routes accept. It is deliberately not a roster — it says who was invited, not who came. `GET /events/{id}/roster` is the other question and lists people; this lists the invitation.

memberCount.description: Members excluding the soft-deleted — the same definition `GET /student-groups` uses, so the number in a picker and the number in the attached panel agree about one group. It is current membership even on a terminal event: the group row is a historical record of what was invited, but this count describes the group as it is now, and the frozen population is EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.Expected.

EventAudienceRequest.description:
The body of `POST /events/{id}/attendees` — §6.3's `{studentIds[], groupIds[]}`.
            


Both lists are optional and both may be sent at once. Sending neither is a no-op rather than an
error: it is what "the organizer cleared the form and saved" looks like, and 400-ing it would say
the request was malformed when it was merely empty.

expected.description:
The event's expected-attendee count after this call — the same number
`GET /events/{id}/summary` reports. Returned here so the UI can show the denominator move as
sections are attached, without a follow-up request.

warnings.description:
Non-fatal observations about what was attached. Empty on the ordinary case. See
`IEventService.AttachAudienceAsync` for why a term mismatch warns rather than refuses.

EventAudienceResultDto.description: What one call to `POST /events/{id}/attendees` did. The `Already` counters exist so idempotency is observable rather than merely true. A re-post returning `{attached: 0, alreadyAttached: 3}` tells a caller its earlier request landed; a bare 200 would leave "did that save?" unanswerable without a second round trip.

every event edited through the UI. Additive on the wire; existing consumers ignore them.
