The two mechanisms coexisting is correct, not an inconsistency to tidy.

studentId.description: The identity to key the offline index by. Stable.

studentNumber.description: The institutional student number. It is not a tap identity and must never be matched against a scanned serial (D-43). The card UID and the student number come from different source columns and have no relationship; a device that falls back to matching the number when a UID misses will attribute a tap to a stranger.

groupIds.description: Which of EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventManifestDto.Groups reach this student, ordinal-ordered. Empty is common and is not an anomaly — it is the individually-attached student, the handful an organizer named by hand on top of the sections. A client that filters by group must keep an "all" or "ungrouped" view, or those students are invisible on the device while being fully expected on the server.

cardUids.description: The student's active card serials, normalized (`CardUid.Normalize` — uppercased, non-alphanumerics stripped) and ordinal-ordered. Normalize a scanned serial the same way before comparing: normalize first, compare second. Strings, never numbers, at every layer. Real serials from the CICSS export are ten decimal digits with significant leading zeros: `0012503301` through a numeric type is `12503301` — a different card that will never match anything — and it breaks identically on both sides of the wire, so nothing anywhere reports an error. Plural, because a reissue leaves the old row active (ADR-001 D-3). A student can legitimately present either card. Empty is today's ordinary case, not an error. The supplied roster carries no RFID column (D-43), so every student currently imports with no card at all. A client whose manifest is entirely cardless must tell the operator the offline cache is unusable rather than silently offering an index that can never hit.

EventManifestAttendeeDto.description: One expected student. Exactly one row per student, however many attached groups reach them.

groups.description: Every §4.7 group attached to this event's audience, ordered by `studentGroupId`. Called `groups` rather than `sections`, matching EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventAudienceDto.`StudentGroups.Type` is wider than "Section" — a college, a programme and a hand-made "SSC Officers" list are all groups — so a field named `sections` would be a lie on three of the values it can carry, and a client that filtered on the name would drop them.

attendees.description: Who is expected, de-duplicated to exactly one row per student, ordered by `studentId`. The de-duplication is the contract, not an implementation detail. Twelve of the fifty-two students in the real roster sit in more than one section (ADR-001 D-1/D-2), so an event that invites two sections of one programme reaches a quarter of them twice. A client keying its offline index by `studentId` against a doubled list either overwrites a row's `groupIds` — losing the second section — or double-counts the denominator it shows on screen. Both look plausible. `attendees.length` equals the `expected` that `GET /events/{id}/summary`, `GET /events/{id}/roster` and `GET /events/{id}/attendees` report for the same event — the same population from the same query, with the soft-deleted excluded the same way (ADR-003 D-15). It is not "approximately the same": a device showing a different denominator from the dashboard beside it is what an operator files as "the system is wrong", and neither number looks wrong on its own. ADR-003 D-19 records what a second implementation of that count costs.

serverTime.description: Our clock when this body was composed. Check it against the device clock before enabling scan mode: if the two differ by more than five minutes, do not scan. Every tap captured past that threshold arrives as `TappedAtOutOfRange` — poison, dropped by the client's own queue, attendance gone. It is the one clock rule that prevents loss rather than reporting it. A 304 carries no body and therefore no `serverTime`; take the offset from the HTTP `Date` header instead. Assuming the previous offset is still valid because the manifest did not change is wrong — the manifest not changing says nothing about the clock. There is deliberately no separate `generatedAt`. The two would be identical today, and a client that treated them as interchangeable would compute its clock offset from a cache-fill time the day a server-side cache lands.

version.description: The `ETag` with the `W/` prefix and the quotes stripped. Opaque: never parse it, never order it, compare it for equality only. It is duplicated into the body because an offline client persists a parsed object and very often not the headers that came with it — and the value it has to send back in `If-None-Match` on the next pull is exactly this one.

EventManifestDto.description: The body of `GET /api/v1/events/{id}/manifest` (D-46) — the offline capture cache a device pulls before it starts scanning, published as the `EventManifest*` schemas in the generated OpenAPI document and frozen with the external mobile developer. This is the invitation, not the roster. It says who is expected and which card resolves to whom; it says nothing about who has already tapped. That is `GET /attendance/live/{eventId}`. A manifest carrying attendance state would read as authoritative on the device, and the one thing this object must never be is authoritative — the server rules on every tap, always. Offline validation against it is display-only and never gating. A tap whose UID is absent from this manifest MUST still be queued and flushed. The server decides; it lands as a walk-in (`isExpected: false`, already modelled by EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventRosterDto, D-20). A client that refuses to capture an unknown card converts "the cache is stale" into "the attendance never existed", and the two are indistinguishable afterwards. Never truncated and never paged. Over `EventManifestLimits.MaxAttendees` this endpoint is a loud `413`, never a partial body.

id.description: The event id every queued tap must carry.

name.description: Prose. Display only — never parsed, and reworded freely.

startAt.description: UTC, and the same field EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventDto publishes — `startAt`, not `startsAt`.

endAt.description: UTC. This is not the capture window, and treating it as one loses taps. The range D-36 actually accepts is EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventManifestEventDto.StartAt/EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventManifestEventDto.EndAt widened by a per-school margin, and that margin is deliberately not published: publishing it invites the client to enforce the window locally and refuse taps the server would have accepted. Queue everything; let the server rule.

graceMinutes.description:
§4.5's Present-versus-Late boundary, published so a device can label its own screen. The server
decides the stored status regardless.

attendanceMode.description: `Single` or `TimeInOut`. An unrecognised value must be treated as `Single` (§4.5's default) — a device that refuses to scan because a future mode was added is worse than one that captures single taps.

status.description:
Always `Open` on a 200: this endpoint serves no other status (see the 409s). Published anyway
so a persisted manifest carries what it was captured against.

EventManifestEventDto.description: The event this manifest is for, in the fields a capture client actually branches on.

studentGroupId.description: The id EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventManifestAttendeeDto.GroupIds refers to. Stable across pulls.

name.description:
Prose. Display only. A derived group's name carries its term — `"BSFS 2-A (2025-2026-1)"` —
which is presentation, not structure; do not parse it back out.

type.description: §4.7's set plus `College`/`Program` (ADR-001 D-1). An unrecognised value must render as a plain group and must never be dropped — otherwise a future group kind silently removes students from the device's filter, and they are fully expected on the server the whole time.

EventManifestGroupDto.description: One §4.7 group attached to the event's audience.

isFrozen.description: True once this event's audience has been snapshotted — both terminal statuses. The published statement that these numbers can no longer move on their own: a later roster import that adds students to an attached section does not change them. It covers `Cancelled` as well as `Closed`, and did not always. Cancelling now writes the resolved audience down exactly as closing does — it simply materializes no absentees — so a cancelled event's denominator is as fixed as a closed one's. Reporting `false` for it would be the same class of plausible-but-wrong published number this phase exists to remove.

expected.description: The invited population: every student in an attached group, plus every individually attached student, de-duplicated. This is the denominator §4.5 and §12 mean, and it is not the length of EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventRosterDto.Entries — a student who tapped without being invited is listed with `IsExpected = false` and is not counted here. While the event is live the soft-deleted are excluded: a student the roster says does not exist cannot be expected to attend. Once EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventRosterDto.IsFrozen they are included, because by then this is a written-down record of who was invited and a student deleted next year must not retroactively shrink a past event's denominator.

notRecorded.description: Expected students with no attendance row at all. While the event is live this is the running absentee list; after a close it is zero, because closing materializes every one of them as an `Absent` record. After a cancellation it is the whole audience, and that is the honest answer: the invitation list was frozen, and nobody attended because the event did not happen.

unexpected.description:
Entries flagged `IsExpected = false` — recorded but never invited. The same number
`GET /events/{id}/summary` reports under the same name, so the two views of one event agree
about how many walk-ins it had.

EventRosterDto.description: `GET /events/{id}/roster` — §6.3's "expected vs present roster" and the source of §12's Absentee Report. The header counts and EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventRosterDto.Entries always reconcile. The buckets are counted over exactly the rows listed, so an operator adding up the roster gets the header. They also match `GET /events/{id}/summary`, which counts the same attendance rows.

isExpected.description:
Whether the event's audience includes this student. False means a walk-in: they have an attendance
record but no invitation. Listed rather than hidden, because the alternative is a roster whose rows
do not add up to the summary an organizer is looking at beside it.

status.description:
The §4.9 status, or `null` for an expected student with no record yet. Null is the absentee
signal before a close; there are none after one.

cardUid.description:
The normalized serial the device sent. It matched no active card in this school at the moment the
tap was decided — which is not the same as "no such card exists now": a card issued afterwards
does not retroactively resolve rows already written.

scannedAt.description:
The device's `tappedAt` for this scan, not the moment the server saw it. For an offline queue
those differ by however long the device was away, and the first is when the person was standing
there.

recordedAt.description: When the server wrote this row. Compare with ScannedAt to see flush lag.

deviceTapId.description:
The device's idempotency key. Present for anything queued offline; a device that omits it cannot
have its retries de-duplicated, which is why the batch path refuses rows without one.

deviceId.description: The device that captured it, where known.

serverOutcome.description:
What the server decided. `CardNotFound` today, and the field exists so that a second
unresolved outcome can be added later without changing the shape of this report.

localOutcome.description: What the device claimed, verbatim and possibly null. Never authoritative. Its value is in disagreeing with ServerOutcome: a device reporting that it found this card while the server could not resolve it is evidence of a stale manifest, a sync that did not run, or a cloned card.

EventScanDto.description: One scan that reached the server and resolved to nobody, as `GET /events/{id}/scans` reports it. Every row here is a scan that is in no other record. A scan whose card resolves becomes an `AttendanceRecord` and is reported by `GET /events/{id}/roster` and the attendance list; it is deliberately absent from this report rather than duplicated into it. This is the remainder — the population that until now existed only as an HTTP response nobody kept.

eventId.description: The event these scans were filed under.

totalScans.description: Every unresolved scan, including repeat presentations of one card.

distinctCards.description:
How many different cards those scans represent.
            


Both numbers are reported because they answer different questions and the gap between them is
itself informative. Forty scans over three cards is somebody presenting a card that is not working
and trying again; forty scans over forty cards is a roster that has not been given its RFID
column.

EventScanLogDto.description:
The unresolved scans for one event, with the counts a reader needs before deciding whether the
list is worth reading.

expected.description: The invited population: students in the event's attached §4.8 groups plus its individually attached students, de-duplicated, excluding the soft-deleted. This used to be the recorded-row count, which made the rate structurally incapable of falling below the share of rows somebody had marked `Absent` by hand, and made an absentee unrepresentable: a student who never taps has no row, so they were not counted as expected either. A number that was always about 100% and meant nothing. Zero means no audience is attached, not "nobody was invited to a well-defined event". Nothing falls back to the old count in that case — a denominator that silently changes definition depending on whether a table is empty is worse than one that is honestly absent. `GET /events/{id}/roster` is where to look: it lists whoever did tap, each flagged `isExpected: false`.

present.description:
Counted over every attendance row on the event, including any belonging to a student the audience
does not name. That is deliberate: these four must reconcile with
`GET /attendance?eventId=` and with the roster, or the summary becomes a fifth opinion.

unexpected.description: Attendees who were recorded but never invited — walk-ins. Counted as people, so it is exactly the number of `GET /events/{id}/roster` entries flagged `isExpected: false`. This is where the over-100% signal went, and it is a better one than the rate was.AttendanceRate used to divide every Present and Late row — walk-ins included — by a denominator that counted only the invited, so twenty-nine expected, twenty-nine present and two tapping alumni read 106.9%. Every underlying row was truthful and the headline number was impossible. Folding the walk-ins into the rate was the wrong place to surface them: it corrupted the one number an operator reads first, and it said "something is off" without saying how many or who. Counting them here says both, and the roster names them.

attendanceRate.description: The share of the invited who turned up: invited students with a `Present` or `Late` record, over Expected, as a percentage to one decimal place. Zero when Expected is zero. It cannot exceed 100, structurally rather than by clamping. Numerator and denominator are both computed over the expected set — the numerator as a SQL `INTERSECT` against it, which is distinct on both sides — so the numerator is a subset of the denominator by construction. No cap is applied and none is needed; a clamp would have hidden the arithmetic rather than fixed it. Walk-ins are therefore not in this number. They are not discarded: see Unexpected, and note that Present and Late still count every row on the event, so the buckets keep reconciling with `GET /attendance?eventId=` while the rate answers the question it is named for.

EventSummaryDto.description: Technical Plan §6.7/§12 — the Event Attendance Summary.

startAt.description:
UTC. Normalized through `UtcTime` on the way in — a bare or offset-bearing JSON date-time is
otherwise compared against a UTC `StartAt` and misjudges Present versus Late by the server's
offset, which is eight hours in Manila.

attendanceMode.description: `Single` or `TimeInOut`; null or blank takes §4.5's `Single` default.

EventWriteRequest.description: The body of `POST /events` and `PUT /events/{id}`. `Status` is deliberately absent.`PATCH /events/{id}/status` is the only door into the column, which is what makes the roster freeze impossible to bypass — an event cannot reach `Closed` without passing through the one code path that materializes its absentees. A `status` field here would be a second door, and the first caller to use it would create a closed event with no frozen roster and no error. `SchoolId` is deliberately absent too. The tenant comes from `ISchoolContext`, not from the request. A caller-supplied `SchoolId` on a write is exactly the hole `KnownDefectTests.A_device_from_another_school_cannot_record_a_tap` is still open on; this endpoint does not add a second one.

LiveOutcomeCode.description:
The `code` returned by `GET /attendance/live/{eventId}` when the poll is refused.
`Ok` never appears in a body — a successful poll is the `AttendanceLiveDto` itself.

On `InvalidCursor`, re-poll with **no** `since` and take a fresh snapshot. The cursor
is refused rather than silently downgraded to a snapshot, because a downgrade would
look like "nothing changed" forever while the client's cursor stayed broken.

| `code` | HTTP |
|---|---|
| `Ok` | 200 |
| `EventNotFound` | 404 |
| `InvalidCursor` | 400 |

email.description:
The login identifier. Trimmed and lower-cased server-side before the lookup, because
`UX_Users_Email` stores the normalized form — a user who types `Admin@…` on a phone
keyboard must not be told their password is wrong.

password.description: The presented password. Never logged, never echoed, never audited — the failure row records the address that was tried and nothing else.

ManualOutcomeCode.description:
The `code` returned by `POST /attendance/manual` — the organizer override, which is
not a device path.

**Frozen published contract on the same terms as `TapOutcomeCode`**, and pinned by the
same kind of test. It travels through the identical `code` field, so one accessor
reads both.

`POST /attendance/manual` deliberately keeps working on a `Closed` event: it is the
only recovery route out of a terminal status.

| `code` | HTTP |
|---|---|
| `Saved` | 200 |
| `EventNotFound` | 404 |
| `StudentNotFound` | 404 |
| `InvalidStatus` | 400 |
| `InvalidNotes` | 400 |

traceId.description:
**On every error body this API produces.** The correlation handle: the distributed
trace id when tracing is on, the per-connection request id otherwise.

Quote it back when reporting a problem — it is the only value that finds the one log
line explaining an otherwise opaque failure.

code.description:
The stable, machine-readable outcome token. **Branch on this, never on `title` or
`detail`** — those are prose written for a person and are reworded freely.

Present on the attendance, students and devices surfaces, and on authentication and
rate-limit refusals. Absent on the events write surface. See the `TapOutcomeCode`,
`ManualOutcomeCode` and `LiveOutcomeCode` schemas for the frozen token tables.

On the attendance surface it is the **same field, with the same values**, that a
success body carries — one accessor works across success and failure alike.

serverTime.description:
The server's UTC clock when this response was produced. Present on tap and
manual-override failures.

It is on rejections deliberately, and it matters most on `TappedAtOutOfRange`: that
response tells a device its clock is wrong, so it has to say what the right one is in
the same body. Compute an offset from it and apply that before enqueueing.

countersReconcile.description:
Whether the counters add up. Exposed rather than left for the caller to compute because it is
the one check an operator runs, and a UI that has to derive it will eventually derive it wrong.

SisImportBatchDto.description:
A batch's summary. The five outcome counters are the reconciliation ADR-001 D-5 exists to make
possible: `InsertedRows + UpdatedRows + FailedRows + SkippedRows == TotalRows`, always.
EAMS.Application.Dtos.SisImportBatchDto.WarningRows is orthogonal — a warned row is already counted in one of the four.

SisImportPreviewDto.description:
What an upload found, before anything is written to the academic tables.
            


The distinct counts are the preview's whole purpose: they are what an operator compares against what
they expect the file to contain, and they are cheap because they come from the staged rows rather
than from a trial run. A file with one course in it is a wrong file, and this is where that is
visible — before the run, not after.

SisImportRowDto.description: One staged source row and what became of it.

SisImportRowEntityDto.description:
One entity a row touched. The answer to "row 214 says Skipped — against what?", which §4.12's single
nullable `StudentId` could not give for a source whose grain spans six entities.

SisImportRunRequest.description: The body of `POST /sis/import/{batchId}/run`. The term is required here even though the batch already carries one. It is a confirmation, and it must match or the run is refused. ADR-001 D-5 names the failure this guards: a wrong term selection misfiles an entire batch, is invisible afterwards (every downstream query is term-scoped, so the data looks fine — it is simply in the wrong year), and is only recoverable by hand. Asking twice, at upload and at the moment of writing, costs one field and turns the mistake into a 409.

StudentCardRequest.description:
The body of `POST /students/{id}/cards` — §6.2's `{cardUid, label}`.
            


The UID is normalized before anything is compared or stored (`CardUid.Normalize`): readers
emit `04:a7:b8:c9`, `04-A7-B8-C9` and `04 a7 b8 c9` for one card, and the stored form
is the only one the filtered unique index can defend.

course.description: Read-only. ADR-001 D-2 derived cache. Present because the students grid renders and filters on it. Sending it back on a write is refused with `FieldIsDerived` rather than ignored — a caller that echoes the object it read would otherwise believe it had saved a section.

StudentDto.description: Technical Plan §4.3, as a client sees it. The name parts and `Gender`/`PhotoUrl` arrived with the §6.2 write surface, and they are not decoration — they are what makes `PUT /students/{id}` usable at all. The PUT is a full replacement of a student's own fields, so a field a client cannot read is a field it cannot send back, and the round trip would blank it. `FullName` is computed and cannot be split back into three columns, so an edit form had no way to populate itself. Additive on the wire; existing consumers ignore them. Same reasoning EAMS.Application.Dtos.EventDto records for `Description`.

items.description:
This page's rows, in the endpoint's documented order. Empty is an ordinary answer — for an empty
filter and for a page past the end alike.

page.description: The 1-based page actually served, which is not necessarily the one requested: an out-of-range `?page=` is clamped and this is where a client sees that it was.

pageSize.description:
The page size actually applied, after the EAMS.Application.Dtos.Paging.MaxPageSize clamp. The field that
makes clamping discoverable rather than silent.

total.description:
Rows matching the filter across every page, counted in the database against the same filter that
produced Items. This is what a grid needs to render a page count; without it a
caller can only discover the end by walking into it.

hasMore.description: Whether another page exists after this one. Derived here rather than left to the client, because the client gets it wrong.`page * pageSize < total` is right and `items.Count == pageSize` is the version people write — which reports a further page whenever the last page happens to be exactly full, so a paging loop makes one extra request every time the total is a multiple of the page size. Computing it once, on the side that already holds the total, is a byte on the wire against a class of off-by-one nobody finds in review.

The two mechanisms coexisting is correct, not an inconsistency to tidy.

type.description:
§4.7's set plus `College`, `Program` and `YearLevel` — `Course`,
`Section`, `Org`, `Custom`, `College`, `Program`, `YearLevel`. What
kind of audience this is, and the axis `GET /student-groups?type=…` narrows by.

sourceType.description:
`Manual` (a person made it) or `Derived` (the projection owns it). The distinction
            matters to a caller: a derived group's membership is rewritten from the academic tables on every
            import, so hand-editing it is not durable, while a manual group is nobody's to reconcile.

sourceEntityType.description:
Which academic concept a derived group projects — `College`, `Program`, `Section`,
`CourseOffering`, `YearLevel` — or `None` on a manual group. `None` is a
sentinel rather than a null so the column stays NOT NULL and the projection's unique index has no
nullable component; a year group carries its own value rather than borrowing that sentinel, because
`None` is what a reader tests to mean "the projection did not build this".

termId.description: The term a derived group belongs to; null on a manual group, which spans terms by nature. Filtering by it is the main reason to filter at all — section names are reused every semester against an entirely different set of students, so "BSFS 2-A" without a term names several distinct cohorts. EAMS.Application.Dtos.StudentGroupDto.Name carries the term for the same reason.

memberCount.description:
Members excluding the soft-deleted, counted in the database as part of the same query. This is the
number an organizer is really choosing on — "invite BSCRIM 2-A" is a different decision at 8
students than at 80 — and a group showing zero is the visible signal that a projection has not run
for its term.

lastSyncedAt.description: When the projection last reconciled this group, stamped on every run including runs that changed nothing — so "synced, no change" is distinguishable from "never synced". Null on a manual group, which the projection never touches.

StudentGroupDto.description: Technical Plan §4.7 `StudentGroups`, as a client sees it — the thing an event audience is actually attached to. `POST /events/{id}/attendees` takes ids from this list. The provenance fields are the reason this list is usable as one picker. ADR-001 D-1 projects colleges, programmes, sections and course offerings into this table as ordinary rows marked EAMS.Application.Dtos.StudentGroupDto.SourceType`Derived`, so an organizer picks "BSFS 2-A (2025-2026-1)" from the same list as "SSC Officers" and nothing downstream learns that one of them was materialized. status.description:
One of `Active` / `Inactive` / `Graduated` (§4.3). Null or blank takes §4.3's
`Active` default, so a create form that has no status field still produces a valid row.

StudentWriteRequest.description: The body of `POST /students` and `PUT /students/{id}`. `Course`, `YearLevel` and `Section` are deliberately absent, and their absence is the whole point of this type. They are the ADR-001 D-2 derived display cache: a student enrolled in two sections cannot be described by a single-valued triple — 12 of the 52 students in the real roster are — so the academic tables are the source of truth and these columns are refreshed from them. A writable field here would be a second, diverging answer to "what section is this student in", and `EamsDbContext`'s cache guard exists because `db.Students.Update(entity)` — the shape a REST PUT handler takes — is the exact path it was built to catch. Absent is not enough on its own, which is what EAMS.Application.Dtos.StudentWriteRequest.UnmappedFields is for. Without it, a client that reads a EAMS.Application.Dtos.StudentDto, edits the name and PUTs the whole object back — the ordinary shape of an edit form — would have its `course`/`section` silently dropped by the deserializer and would believe they were saved. Capturing what we did not model lets the service refuse the request by name instead. `SchoolId` and `IsDeleted` are absent too. The tenant comes from `ISchoolContext`, never from the request (see `EventWriteRequest` for the same rule); deletion is `DELETE /students/{id}`, so there is one door into the flag rather than two. `SisExternalId`, `LastSyncedAt` and `AlternateEmail` are absent because they belong to the §10 import pipeline — a manual edit must not be able to claim a student came from the SIS, and a PUT that omitted them would blank an importer's work.

clientClockAt.description: The device's own clock at the moment it sent this batch. It is measured, not validated. Its difference from our clock is pure skew — unlike a row's `tappedAt`, which also carries however long that row sat in the queue — so it is the one value that can tell a drifted device from a slow flush. A batch is never refused because of it: the clock rules that do refuse (D-36) are per row and apply to `tappedAt` alone. This is logged, and a client that omits it simply is not measured.

taps.description: The queued taps, in whatever order the queue holds them. Each row is exactly the EAMS.Application.Dtos.TapRequest that `POST /attendance/tap` takes, `eventId` included. `eventId` stays per row rather than being hoisted onto the envelope, and that is a decision rather than an oversight: a device that switched events while offline holds a queue spanning both, and hoisting would force it to either split the flush or lie about one of them. Null and empty are the same thing and both are a 200 with no results — "the queue had nothing to send" is not a malformed request. The element type is nullable, and that annotation is load-bearing rather than pedantic.`{"taps": [null]}` is valid JSON, and `System.Text.Json` puts a null in the list: ASP.NET's implicit-required-from-nullable-reference-types covers bound parameters and properties and never covers collection elements, so nothing upstream rejects it. Declared non-nullable, the compiler agreed the elements could not be null and the batch loop dereferenced one straight into a `NullReferenceException` — a batch-level 500 that §8.2's queue retries forever. Saying `TapRequest?` is what makes the null a case the code has to answer.

TapBatchRequest.description:
The body of `POST /attendance/tap/batch` — Technical Plan §8.2's offline queue flush, and the
shape frozen with the external mobile developer, published as the `TapBatchRequest` /
`TapBatchResult` schemas in the generated OpenAPI document (Phase 4d, D-31).

rejected.description:
The rest. A rejected row is one this API will refuse identically on every retry — the client drops
it and, per the published guidance, stops the queue rather than skipping past it.

serverTime.description:
Read once for the whole batch. A client computes its clock offset from this exactly as it does from
a single tap's `serverTime`.

results.description: One entry per submitted tap, in the request's array order, so `results[i].index == i`. That is a stronger guarantee than the published contract asks for, and it is free: rows are processed in ascending `tappedAt` and then written back into their original slots. It is stated because the cheap client is the one that zips `results` against `taps` positionally, and a contract that merely says "correlate by index" would let a future change break that client silently. Correlating by EAMS.Application.Dtos.TapBatchRowResult.Index or by EAMS.Application.Dtos.TapBatchRowResult.DeviceTapId works regardless and is what the document tells clients to do.

TapBatchResult.description: The body of a well-formed `POST /attendance/tap/batch`. Always HTTP 200. Not 207 Multi-Status, and the reason is about clients rather than about correctness. Proxies and HTTP libraries handle 207 inconsistently, and — the part that actually bites — a client that sees any non-2xx transport status is liable to retry the whole batch. Retrying is safe here, because every row is idempotent, but it is pure waste when 197 of 200 rows landed. The batch status describes the batch; each row's EAMS.Application.Dtos.TapBatchRowResult.Status describes that tap. A batch-level `4xx` is transport, auth or size only — a malformed body, `BatchTooLarge`, a missing or bad key, a revoked one. Nothing about the content of a row can produce one. On a `5xx` the client retries the whole batch, and that is always safe — every row is keyed by `deviceTapId` and index-guarded, so a resend converges on the same rows however much of the first attempt landed. The published contract words this as "a 5xx means nothing was committed", which is stronger than what per-row commits provide; see `AttendanceService.TapBatchAsync` for the discrepancy and why idempotency rather than atomicity is the property the client actually depends on.

results.message: No active card matches that UID.

index.description: The row's position in the request's `taps` array — not its position in the order the server processed it, and not necessarily its position in `results` either, though today those two agree. See EAMS.Application.Dtos.TapBatchResult.Results.

deviceTapId.description:
The row's idempotency key, echoed back. The second correlation handle: a client that has lost track
of its own array can still reconcile, which matters because the array is exactly what a crashed
client no longer has.

code.description: The frozen outcome token — the same value, from the same table, that `POST /attendance/tap` returns for the identical tap. Branch on this.

status.description: The HTTP status this row would have received as a single tap. The transport status is always 200 for a well-formed batch, so this is the field §8.2's queue reads to decide drop, stop or retry — the same 2xx/4xx reasoning it already applies to a single tap's status line.

message.description:
Prose, never parsed, and present on success rows as well as failures — the same string the single
endpoint puts in `TapResult.message` or in a problem body's `detail`.

TapBatchRowResult.description: One row of a batch response.

TapOutcomeCode.description:
The `code` returned by `POST /attendance/tap` and by every row of
`POST /attendance/tap/batch`, on success bodies and RFC 7807 problem bodies alike.

**This list is frozen published contract.** A rename here is a breaking change for a
client we cannot recompile, and the symptom is a queue that quietly stops reconciling
rather than anything that looks like a failure. A build-gating test pins it.

Queue guidance: a `2xx` row is done — drop it. A `4xx` row will be refused identically
forever — stop retrying rather than skipping past it, and flush strictly in order.
`BatchTooLarge` is the one exception: chunk to `maxBatchRows` and resend.

| `code` | HTTP |
|---|---|
| `Recorded` | 200 |
| `DuplicateIgnored` | 200 |
| `CheckedOut` | 200 |
| `AlreadyRecorded` | 200 |
| `EventNotFound` | 404 |
| `EventNotOpen` | 400 |
| `CardNotFound` | 404 |
| `DeviceNotRegistered` | 404 |
| `DeviceMismatch` | 400 |
| `TappedAtOutOfRange` | 400 |
| `TappedAtOutsideEventWindow` | 400 |
| `DeviceTapIdRequired` | 400 |
| `BatchTooLarge` | 400 |

localOutcome.description: What the device concluded about this card from its own cached manifest, before it knew what the server would say. Optional; omit it and nothing changes. It never influences the outcome, and a test pins that. The server resolves the card itself and rules on the tap exactly as it would have without this field. A device that lied — or that is simply running a stale manifest — cannot mark anyone present, absent, or unknown by saying so. Its purpose is the disagreement. A device that says it found a card the server cannot resolve is evidence of something real: a stale cache, a sync that did not run, a cloned card, a reader misreading. That case leaves no trace otherwise, because `CardNotFound` is a rejection rather than a row, and it is the case most worth seeing. Free text, stored verbatim, never parsed into a closed set. The vocabulary is the mobile client's and is not fixed yet. Validating it would mean a value we have not seen could 400 an entire flush — a field that exists only for reporting must never be able to reject attendance. Anything longer than `TapRequestLimits.MaxLocalOutcomeLength` is truncated rather than refused, for the same reason.

success.description:
**Deprecated — read `code` instead.** Retained for clients already reading it; the
behaviour is unchanged and it will not be removed without notice.

It carries no information `code` does not. It is `false` on exactly the outcomes that
arrive as a `4xx`, and a `4xx` is an RFC 7807 problem body that has no `success` member —
so in every body where you can actually see this field it is `true`.

message.description: Prose. Never parse it. It is written for a person reading a log or a kiosk screen and is reworded whenever the wording is wrong; Code is what a client branches on.

code.description: The stable outcome token — `nameof` the EAMS.Application.Abstractions.TapOutcome or EAMS.Application.Abstractions.ManualOutcome member this response carries (Phase 4c, D-37). Why the field is `code` and not `outcome`. A failure is an RFC 7807 problem body, which already carries `code` everywhere else in this API (`StudentsController`, `DevicesController`, the device-key handler, the rate limiter). Naming the success field the same thing means one accessor — `body.code` — works across success and failure alike, which is the whole of what the mobile client asked for: today all four tap successes are an indistinguishable 200 whose only differentiator is the prose above, so reconciling a flushed queue against what actually landed is impossible. These token names are published contract. Renaming `DuplicateIgnored` is a breaking change for a consumer we cannot recompile, so `TapOutcomeContractTests` enumerates the enum against a frozen list and fails the build rather than letting a rename ship quietly.

serverTime.description:
The server's UTC clock at the moment this response was produced. The published contract promises it
on every response and the client computes a clock offset from it before enqueueing — which is the
half of D-36 that lets a drifted device correct itself instead of having its taps refused. It is on
rejections too, and most of all on `TappedAtOutOfRange`: that is precisely the response whose
reader needs to know what time we think it is.

TapResult.description:
The body of `POST /attendance/tap` and `POST /attendance/manual` on every path that
produced a record. Failures carry the same two machine-readable fields in an RFC 7807 body instead
— see `AttendanceController`.

isCurrent.description: Nullable so that omitting it is a refusal rather than a decision. A non-nullable `bool` deserializes a missing member to `false`, which on this route means "clear the current term" — a client that forgot the field would silently retire the school's term and get a `200` for it. Send `true` to make this term current, or `false` to retire it; there is no default. `false` is the whole of "retiring a term", and it is why this route is not named `make-current`: D-53 offers no deletion, because a term with a batch imported against it cannot be removed without data loss. Clearing the flag leaves zero current terms, which is an ordinary state the read surface already answers for — `GET /academic/terms/current` 404s and `GET /academic/course-offerings` returns an empty page.

At most one term per school carries this, enforced by a filtered unique index rather than by
convention. `GET /academic/terms/current` is the direct route to it; this flag is here so a
list rendering does not need a second request to mark the row.

TermDto.description: Technical Plan §4 / ADR-001 D-1 `Terms`, as a client sees it. EAMS.Application.Dtos.TermDto.StartsOn and EAMS.Application.Dtos.TermDto.EndsOn are dates, not instants, and stay that way on the wire. A term boundary is a calendar date in the school's own timezone — it has no time of day, and serializing it as a UTC instant would shift it by eight hours in Manila and make "does this term contain today" answerable two different ways. They publish as `YYYY-MM-DD`.

items.description:
This page's rows, in the endpoint's documented order. Empty is an ordinary answer — for an empty
filter and for a page past the end alike.

page.description: The 1-based page actually served, which is not necessarily the one requested: an out-of-range `?page=` is clamped and this is where a client sees that it was.

pageSize.description:
The page size actually applied, after the EAMS.Application.Dtos.Paging.MaxPageSize clamp. The field that
makes clamping discoverable rather than silent.

total.description:
Rows matching the filter across every page, counted in the database against the same filter that
produced Items. This is what a grid needs to render a page count; without it a
caller can only discover the end by walking into it.

hasMore.description: Whether another page exists after this one. Derived here rather than left to the client, because the client gets it wrong.`page * pageSize < total` is right and `items.Count == pageSize` is the version people write — which reports a further page whenever the last page happens to be exactly full, so a paging loop makes one extra request every time the total is a multiple of the page size. Computing it once, on the side that already holds the total, is a byte on the wire against a class of off-by-one nobody finds in review.

TermDtoPagedResult.description: One page of an admin list read, plus what the caller needs to ask for the next one. Every §6.2/§6.3 admin list returns this; `GET /attendance/live/{eventId}` deliberately does not. That endpoint pages by cursor (`since`/`cursor`/`hasMore`) because it is a polling delta rather than a list — a client asks "what changed after this point", not "give me rows 40 to 60" — and its shape is frozen published contract under D-29/D-30/D-42. Offset paging over a live feed also drops rows: an insert below the cursor shifts every subsequent row up by one and the next page skips it. The two mechanisms coexisting is correct, not an inconsistency to tidy.

startsOn.description:
Optional, and normally absent — the SIS export has no term-date columns, so a real term carries
neither date. Supplied as `YYYY-MM-DD`: a term boundary is a calendar date in the school's own
timezone and has no time of day.

endsOn.description: Optional. If both dates are supplied, this one may not fall before StartsOn.

TermWriteRequest.description: The body of `POST /academic/terms` and `PUT /academic/terms/{id}` (D-53). EAMS.Application.Dtos.TermWriteRequest.Code is stored exactly as typed. It is the one natural key in the academic layer that is authored by a person rather than scraped from a spreadsheet cell, so there is no dirt to clean and `AcademicKey` never touches it. A value with leading or trailing whitespace is a `400` rather than a silent trim — see EAMS.Domain.TermText for why refusing beats normalizing here. `SchoolId` is deliberately absent, exactly as it is on `EventWriteRequest` and `DeviceWriteRequest`: the tenant comes from EAMS.Application.Abstractions.ISchoolContext, never from the request. `IsCurrent` is deliberately absent too, and that is not symmetry for its own sake. Moving the flag is a two-row operation guarded by a filtered unique index (`UX_Terms_SchoolId_Current`), so it is `PATCH /academic/terms/{id}/current` — the same split `PATCH /events/{id}/status` draws for the same reason. It also keeps the create path's unique-violation arm unambiguous: with the current flag out of the body, the only index a create can possibly break is `UX_Terms_SchoolId_Code`, so answering `TermCodeExists` is a fact rather than a guess between two indexes.

DeviceKey.description:
The kiosk / capture credential, scoped to `attendance.capture` and nothing else.

Send the **entire header value including the scheme word**:

```
Authorization: DeviceKey eams_dk_<keyId>_<secret>
```

Issued once by `POST /api/v1/devices` and never retrievable afterwards — the server stores
only a hash. Store it in the platform keystore (`expo-secure-store` / Android Keystore),
never in `AsyncStorage`. Lose it and rotate with `POST /api/v1/devices/{id}/regenerate-key`.

Case is significant and lower-case is the only accepted form for the token itself.

Failures: `401 DeviceKeyMissing` / `DeviceKeyMalformed` / `DeviceKeyInvalid`,
`403 DeviceKeyRevoked` / `DeviceInactive`, `429 RateLimited` (honour `Retry-After`).
`DeviceKeyInvalid` deliberately does not distinguish an unknown key id from a wrong secret.
DeviceKey.name: Authorization

Bearer.description:
The human credential. Obtained from `POST /api/v1/auth/login` and sent on every call:

```
Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>
```

**Fifteen-minute lifetime.** Hold it in memory — never in `localStorage`, and never in a
cookie. Renew it with `POST /api/v1/auth/refresh`, which reads the `eams_rt` httpOnly
cookie the login set; the refresh token is never in a request or response body.

The token carries `sub` (`user:<guid>`), `school_id`, and one `perm` claim per effective
permission, resolved through the caller's roles at issue. There is deliberately no role
claim: authorization in this system is permission-based.

`POST /api/v1/auth/refresh` and `POST /api/v1/auth/logout` additionally require the
`X-CSRF-Token` header, echoing the readable `eams_csrf` cookie. No other endpoint does —
they authenticate with this header, which a cross-site page cannot set.

Failures: `401 InvalidCredentials` / `SessionMissing` / `SessionExpired`,
`403 CsrfTokenInvalid`, `429 RateLimited` (honour `Retry-After`).

tags.name: Academic
tags.description: ADR-001 D-1's academic layer over HTTP — reads, plus D-53's three term-administration writes and nothing else.

tags.name: Auth
tags.description: Technical Plan §6.1 / §11 — human authentication (Phase 6b). This is the first and only surface in the API that a person authenticates against, and adding it changes nothing about any other endpoint. ADR-001 D-6's staged cutover is unchanged: every route outside `/auth` is still open and unauthenticated, `[HasPermissionNotEnforced]` still enforces nothing, and `[assembly: AuthorizationNotEnforced]` is still present. Turning those on is a later phase, and `AuthStagedCutoverTests` asserts the invariant rather than leaving it to be assumed. Two credentials now reach this host and they never mix. A kiosk sends `Authorization: DeviceKey …` and is scoped to `attendance.capture`; a person sends `Authorization: Bearer …` and holds whatever their roles grant. Both emit the same claim types (EAMS.Api.Authorization.EamsClaimTypes), so the authorization layer cannot tell them apart — which is exactly what `DeviceKeyHandler` was built for and why this phase is additive. Where the tokens live. The access token is returned in the body and held in memory by the SPA; the refresh token is an `httpOnly` cookie the browser stores and this API never reads from a body. That is drift from §6.1 and the reasoning is in EAMS.Api.Authentication.AuthCookies.

tags.name: Devices
tags.description: Technical Plan §6.6 — devices (Phase 4a design, D-25). Only one action on this controller is gated: `heartbeat`. It is the one a device calls about itself. Everything else here is an administrator's surface and stays open under ADR-001 D-6 with a declared-but-inert `devices.*` permission, exactly like students and events — Phase 4b narrowed the open surface to four endpoints, it did not roll authorization out.

tags.name: EventManifest
tags.description: The device-facing half of the events resource: `GET /events/{id}/manifest`, the offline capture cache a kiosk or handset pulls before it starts scanning (D-46). Its own controller rather than one more action on `EventsController`, and that is a deliberate split. Every action there is `events.read` or `events.write` and is open under ADR-001 D-6; this one authenticates a device and carries `attendance.capture`. One action with a different principal type in the middle of an administrative controller is a review hazard in both directions — a reader skimming `EventsController` would read the whole file as open, and an action added later to a capture-only controller inherits capture auth rather than landing open by accident. The route is identical either way; only the file is different. `events.read` is rejected outright as the permission for this. A device holding it could read every event and every roster in the school, which is exactly the blast radius a stolen kiosk key must not have. §11 scopes device keys to `attendance.capture` and nothing else, so this endpoint is already pre-authorized by the credential a capture device holds — and minting an `events.manifest` code would repeat D-45, forcing Phase 6 to grant two codes for one capability.

tags.name: SisImport
tags.description: Technical Plan §10 — the school-year roster import. Every endpoint is decorated `sis.import` and every endpoint is open.EAMS.Api.Authorization.HasPermissionNotEnforcedAttribute enforces nothing (ADR-001 D-6); the decoration records what Phase 6 must demand. That matters more here than anywhere else in this API: these four endpoints read and write the full roster of every student in the institution, including their names and institutional e-mail addresses, and the upload endpoint writes to the academic tables. This system must not be exposed beyond local/development use until §11 lands.
